chapter: American Jazz Orchestra, conducting and teaching
title: New School classes, Manhattan School teaching, WBGO and Sirius radio
summary: Teaching, radio at WBGO, and Kenny Washington's Sirius programming.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: please if you want, take my class, I really don’t care. I don’t have time for it right now. So I called up and I started designing my own classes there, which would cover kind of like Ellington and Brahms, and I would take them through a Brahms symphony for a month or two, and then an Ellington extended work, and look for the intersections in terms of the narrative structure of composition and orchestration. I was teaching myself this stuff and getting paid for it. In the very first class at the New School for doing this, I brought in a Brahms string quartet, this kid sat down at the piano — and you know the string quartets with the alto clef and all the funny clefs, just, it was Brad Meldeau. And he just sat down and kind of sight read this. So I said if this is a typical student you know my God. Well that led to eventually teaching at Manhattan School of Music. I took that course over there for graduate students and I was there for about ten years. I mean on my epitaph it should say “Loren Schoenberg, Adjunct to the World.” You know? Because I taught at every school, never a full time faculty, never health coverage or anything. But anyway, I taught there for a long time. And then at the same time I was doing I mean I had done radio. I mean I had done college radio. And then I wound up kind of becoming a fill in radio announcer at WGBO because there was a show called “Jazz from the Archives” with Dan Morgenstern and Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote. And I was kind of like an adopted son or something. So I started doing these shows with them. No money, but a lot of fun and interviewing people but doing a lot of historical shows. And that led to Kenny Washington was hired by Sirius Satellite Radio to take over all these jazz programming in the early days of satellite radio. So Kenny, I mean this is another untold story but he did such a job of digitizing thousands of pieces of Swing Era jazz and 50s era jazz too. And he created a database, this is before people knew what they were doing. He didn’t do it himself but he dictated to a computer guy at Sirius to have the computer program music based on an algorithm of tempo, key, if it modulates, you know, major, minor, big band, small band, so you press a button and you’ve got the greatest sets of music you ever heard in your life with all these weird juxtapositions but that made for great changes of tempo and key all the time. So I was doing that. And you asked a question about the Jazz Museum and we’re just going to get there now.
